beats.narration: Begin by framing The Disciplined Solution Framework as a question about inputs, decisions, and observable results. A disciplined solution states inputs and outputs, proves correctness, and then analyzes time and space. Consider this worked case: Sorting an array: Input is an unordered list of numbers; Output is the same list in non-decreasing order; Correctness is proved by loop invariants; Complexity is O(n log n) via divide-and-conquer. Trace each intermediate state in the example, connect it to the formal claim, and verify that the final result satisfies the stated condition. List the givens before choosing a method, because an unstated assumption can change the conclusion. This establishes the vocabulary and scope needed for the remaining sections.
beats.title: The Disciplined Solution Framework
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a flowchart with three boxes labeled 'Define I/O', 'Prove Correctness', and 'Analyze Resources' connected by arrows.

beats.narration: Now define Asymptotic Notation and Growth precisely enough that another learner could test the definition. Asymptotic notation describes how resource use grows with input size. Consider this worked case: If an algorithm performs 5n + 3 operations, its asymptotic growth is Θ(n), meaning it scales linearly with input size. Trace each intermediate state in the example, connect it to the formal claim, and verify that the final result satisfies the stated condition. Separate the formal definition from an implementation detail, then identify what evidence would distinguish them. A precise definition makes later examples easier to evaluate and revise.
beats.title: Asymptotic Notation and Growth
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Plot a line graph with 'Input Size (n)' on the x-axis and 'Operations' on the y-axis, showing a straight line rising from (1,8) to (10,53).

beats.narration: With the foundation in place, examine how Loop Invariants for Correctness operates in a concrete sequence. A loop invariant supports a proof by initialization, maintenance, and termination. Consider this worked case: In bubble sort, the invariant 'the first i elements are sorted' holds before the loop (i=0), is maintained by swapping adjacent out-of-order elements, and guarantees the whole array is sorted when i=n. Trace each intermediate state in the example, connect it to the formal claim, and verify that the final result satisfies the stated condition. Follow every arrow in order and name the state before and after each transition. The trace converts an abstract statement into an inspectable sequence.
beats.title: Loop Invariants for Correctness
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Draw a loop diagram with an oval labeled 'i from 0 to n-1' and a rectangle inside showing 'swap if a[j] > a[j+1]', with a side note: 'Invariant: first i elements sorted'.

beats.narration: Next, compare the choices involved in Divide-and-Conquer Strategy and make the decision criteria explicit. Divide-and-conquer algorithms split a problem, solve subproblems, and combine their results. Consider this worked case: Merge sort divides an array into two halves, recursively sorts each half, then merges the two sorted halves in linear time. Trace each intermediate state in the example, connect it to the formal claim, and verify that the final result satisfies the stated condition. Compare alternatives against the same constraints so the evaluation does not move the goalposts. Using shared criteria turns a preference into a defensible technical choice.
beats.title: Divide-and-Conquer Strategy
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a binary tree where the root is 'Array', left child is 'Sort Left Half', right child is 'Sort Right Half', and a bottom node labeled 'Merge'.

beats.narration: Apply Recurrences and Their Solutions to a worked situation instead of treating it as an isolated definition. Recurrences describe the cost of recursive algorithms. Consider this worked case: The recurrence T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n for merge sort solves to T(n) = Θ(n log n) via the Master Theorem. Trace each intermediate state in the example, connect it to the formal claim, and verify that the final result satisfies the stated condition. Work from the concrete inputs to the result, checking units, types, or invariants at each step. The worked case shows both how to apply the method and how to check it.
beats.title: Recurrences and Their Solutions
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Display the equation T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n in a centered box, with a small arrow pointing to 'Solution: Θ(n log n)'.

beats.narration: Examine the tradeoffs in Core Data Structures: Lists, Stacks, Queues, including what improves and what becomes more difficult. Lists represent ordered sequences with position-based operations. Consider this worked case: A stack of plates: the last plate placed is the first one removed; a queue of customers: the first person in line is served first. Trace each intermediate state in the example, connect it to the formal claim, and verify that the final result satisfies the stated condition. State the benefit, the cost, and the condition under which the tradeoff is acceptable. Making the tradeoff visible prevents a local improvement from hiding a larger cost.
beats.title: Core Data Structures: Lists, Stacks, Queues
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Draw three side-by-side diagrams: a horizontal line with numbered dots (list), a vertical stack of circles (stack), and a horizontal line with arrows pointing right (queue).

beats.narration: Stress-test the reasoning around Trees and Hierarchical Representation with an edge case and identify which assumption controls the outcome. Trees represent hierarchical relationships and support recursive traversals. Consider this worked case: A binary search tree stores keys so that left children are smaller and right children are larger, enabling O(log n) search on balanced trees. Trace each intermediate state in the example, connect it to the formal claim, and verify that the final result satisfies the stated condition. Change one assumption at a time and observe which part of the reasoning no longer holds. The edge case reveals the boundary of the claim without discarding the useful core idea.
beats.title: Trees and Hierarchical Representation
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Render a small binary tree with root '5', left child '2', right child '8', and their respective children, labeling edges with '<' and '>'.

beats.narration: Use Hash Tables and Collision Strategies to diagnose a failure by separating symptoms, causes, and corrective action. Hash tables map keys to locations and require a collision strategy. Consider this worked case: With hash function h(k) = k mod 7, keys 10 and 17 both map to index 3; chaining stores both in a linked list at that index. Trace each intermediate state in the example, connect it to the formal claim, and verify that the final result satisfies the stated condition. Locate the first point where observed behavior diverges from expected behavior, then test the smallest plausible cause. The diagnosis is strongest when another person can reproduce the observation and the test.
beats.title: Hash Tables and Collision Strategies
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show an array of 7 buckets; bucket 3 contains two circles labeled '10' and '17' connected by a small line indicating a linked list.

beats.narration: Connect Graph Representations and Traversal to the earlier ideas and explain how the pieces work as one system. Graph algorithms operate on vertices and edges to answer reachability, ordering, connectivity, and path questions. Consider this worked case: In a directed graph, a depth-first search (DFS) explores all reachable vertices from a start node, useful for topological ordering. Trace each intermediate state in the example, connect it to the formal claim, and verify that the final result satisfies the stated condition. Explain each connection explicitly and verify that information retains the same meaning across representations. The synthesis matters only if every connection remains supported by the original evidence.
beats.title: Graph Representations and Traversal
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Draw a simple directed graph with three nodes (A→B, B→C, A→C) and label it 'Adjacency List: A:[B,C], B:[C], C:[]'.

beats.narration: Finish with Practical Analysis Checklist as a practical checklist that can guide a new analysis. Algorithm analysis connects a precise problem specification to a correctness argument and resource bounds. Consider this worked case: For Dijkstra's shortest path: define input as weighted graph and output as distance array; prove correctness via loop invariant that visited nodes have optimal distances; analyze time as O((V+E) log V). Trace each intermediate state in the example, connect it to the formal claim, and verify that the final result satisfies the stated condition. For each checklist item, record the evidence, the remaining uncertainty, and the next verification step. The result is a repeatable procedure, not a conclusion that depends on memory or intuition.
beats.title: Practical Analysis Checklist
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Present a checklist graphic with four tick boxes labeled 'Define I/O', 'Prove Correctness', 'Analyze Time', 'Analyze Space'.

sources.excerpt: This course provides an introduction to the design and analysis of algorithms. It covers a variety of classical algorithms and data structures and their complexity and will equip students with the intellectual tools to design, analyze, implement, and evaluate their own algorithms. Prerequisites:(CSCI-243 and (CSCI-262 or CSCI-263)) or (SWEN-262 and MATH-241) or equivalent courses. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Fall, Spring, Summer

sources.author: MIT OpenCourseWare
sources.excerpt: Algorithm analysis connects a precise problem specification to a correctness argument and resource bounds. Asymptotic notation describes how resource use grows with input size. A loop invariant supports a proof by initialization, maintenance, and termination. Divide-and-conquer algorithms split a problem, solve subproblems, and combine their results. Recurrences describe the cost of recursive algorithms. Graph algorithms operate on vertices and edges to answer reachability, ordering, connectivity, and path questions. Dynamic programming records solutions to overlapping subproblems. Core methods include sorting, hashing, trees, graphs, shortest paths, and dynamic programming. A disciplined solution states inputs and outputs, proves correctness, and then analyzes time and space.

sources.author: OpenDSA Project
sources.excerpt: OpenDSA presents data structures and algorithms through executable visualizations and exercises. Lists represent ordered sequences with position-based operations. Stacks use last-in, first-out access, while queues use first-in, first-out access. Trees represent hierarchical relationships and support recursive traversals. Hash tables map keys to locations and require a collision strategy. Graphs can be represented with adjacency structures for traversal and path algorithms. Automata and formal languages describe machines, accepted strings, and computational limits. Representation choices and invariants determine which operations are efficient and which errors are possible.
